The name "Boston" was given to the settlement by Isaac Johnson after his hometown of Boston, Lincolnshire, England.
William Blaxton was the first European to live in what would become Boston.
Isaac Johnson invited one of the leaders of the Puritans, Isaac Johnson, to cross Back Bay from Charlestown and share the peninsula with them.
The Puritans made the crossing in September 1630.
Puritan influence on Boston began even before the settlement was founded with the 1629 Cambridge Agreement.
The Massachusetts Bay Colony was created by the 1629 Cambridge Agreement.
John Winthrop was the first governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony.
Boston's economy stagnated in the decades prior to the Revolution.
New York City and Philadelphia had surpassed Boston in wealth by the mid-18th century.
The British army attempted a cannon barrage for two hours during their evacuation from Boston on March 21, 1776.
The British Army left Boston on March 17, 1876, marking "Evacuation Day".
Boston's long seafaring tradition helped make it one of the nation's busiest ports in the early 19th century.
The Embargo Act of 1807 and the War of 1812 significantly curtailed foreign trade in Boston's harbor.
Manufacturing became an important component of Boston's economy by the mid-19th century.
Small rivers bordering Boston facilitated shipment of goods and led to a proliferation of mills and factories.
A dense network of railroads furthered the region's industry and commerce.
Boston flourished culturally as well, admired for its rarefied literary life and generous artistic patronage.
Members of old Boston families were regarded as the nation's social and cultural elites.
The city reacted negatively to the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850.
Anthony Burns attempted to escape to freedom in 1854.
Boston was chartered as a city on March 19, 1822.
At the time Boston was chartered as a city, the population was about 46,226 and the area of the city was only 4.8 sq mi (12 km²).
The city tripled its area through land reclamation by filling in marshes, mud flats, and gaps between wharves along the waterfront.
Reclamation projects created significant parts of the South End, West End, Financial District, and Chinatown.
The Great Boston Fire of 1872 led to workers using building rubble as landfill along the downtown waterfront.
Almost 600 acres (240 ha) of brackish Charles River marshlands west of Boston Common were filled with gravel brought by rail from Needham Heights.
Boston annexed several towns and neighborhoods, including South Boston, East Boston, Roxbury, Dorchester, Brighton, West Roxbury, Charlestown, and Hyde Park.
The city experienced significant gentrification in the 20th century, during which affluent Whites moved into formerly non-White areas.
By 2010, the non-White population had rebounded due to increased efforts to make more affordable housing available.
Boston's economy began to recover after 30 years of economic downturn by the 1970s.
A large number of high-rises were constructed in the Financial District and Back Bay during this period.
Hospitals such as Massachusetts General Hospital, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, and Brigham and Women's Hospital lead the nation in medical innovation and patient care.

Schools such as Boston Architectural College, Boston University, Harvard Medical School, Tufts University School of Medicine, Northeastern University, Massachusetts College of Art and Design, Wentworth Institute of Technology, Berklee College of Music, and the Boston Conservatory attract students to the area.
The Charles River in front of Boston's Back Bay neighborhood was photographed by James Wallace Black in 1860.
Boston is an intellectual, technological, and political center.

The Charles River separates Boston's Allston-Brighton, Fenway-Kenmore, and Back Bay neighborhoods from Watertown and Cambridge.
The Neponset River forms the boundary between Boston's southern neighborhoods and Quincy and Milton.
The Mystic River separates Charlestown from Chelsea and Everett.
Chelsea Creek and Boston Harbor separate East Boston from Downtown, the North End, and the Seaport.
Boston is located within the Boston Basin ecoregion.
Forests in Boston are mainly transition hardwoods such as oak-hickory mixed with white pine.
Sea-level rise is a major concern for the city government due to its coastal location built largely on fill.
A climate action plan from 2019 anticipates sea-level rise of 2 ft (1 m) to more than 7 ft (2 m) by the end of the 21st century.

Many older buildings in certain areas of Boston are supported by wooden piles driven into the area's fill, which remain sound if submerged but are subject to dry rot if exposed to air for long periods.
Groundwater levels have been dropping in many areas of the city due to an increase in rainwater discharged directly into sewers rather than absorbed by the ground.
The Boston Groundwater Trust coordinates monitoring groundwater levels throughout the city via a network of public and private monitoring wells.
Boston developed a climate action plan covering carbon reduction in buildings, transportation, and energy use.
The first such plan was commissioned in 2007 with updates released in 2011, 2014, and 2019.

This plan includes the Building Energy Reporting and Disclosure Ordinance requiring larger city buildings to disclose yearly energy and water use statistics and partake in an energy assessment every five years.
A separate initiative, Resilient Boston Harbor, lays out neighborhood-specific recommendations for coastal resilience.
The city's average window for freezing temperatures is November 9 through April 5.
Official temperature records have ranged from -18°F (-28°C) on February 9, 1934, to 104°F (40°C) on July 4, 1911.
The record cold daily maximum is 2°F (-17°C) on December 30, 1917.
The record warm daily minimum is 83°F (28°C) on both August 2, 1975, and July 21, 2019.
Boston averages 43.6 in (1,110 mm) of precipitation a year with 49.2 in (125 cm) of snowfall per season.
Most snowfall occurs from mid-November through early April.
